explanation: On a congested road hazards can appear from any side, so the duty of care requires scanning all around with a peripheral check, keeping a safe gap in every direction, and choosing a controllable speed rather than just watching the car ahead.

Braking should be finished before the tires start turning through a bend, since braking mid-curve reduces the grip available for cornering and can trigger a skid; slowing before entry keeps the car's speed matched to the curve throughout.
Right-of-way rules only say who is supposed to yield; they don't guarantee the other driver actually will, so a driver must stay alert and ready to react even when technically entitled to go first.

A vehicle already committed to a turn across your path may not be able to stop safely, so slowing or stopping to let it clear the junction avoids a collision, which fits the general duty to adapt to what other road users are actually doing.

Checking the mirrors first means traffic behind won't be surprised by your braking, while easing off speed and being ready to stop lets you respond safely to the hazard shown, matching the defensive-driving principle of building in a margin before trouble develops.

Children's movements are unpredictable, so the duty of care calls for checking behind you, cutting speed, and being ready to stop completely, rather than relying on a horn or a quick swerve to get past them.

Cyclists can be pushed off line by passing air currents or road defects, so the rule for overtaking them is to slow down, leave a generous sideways gap, and keep watching their movement throughout the pass instead of squeezing by quickly.

When children are playing on the roadway, the driver's duty of care means taking every reasonable precaution to avoid endangering them, rather than honking and expecting them to clear the road on their own.

Because children can dart onto the road without warning, a driver must slow down, keep tracking their movement, and stay ready to stop, instead of assuming they will stay clear just because a vehicle is approaching.

Even without a marked crossing or a play-street sign, the general duty of care obliges a driver to watch children on both sides of the road, slow down, and stop if necessary, since missing formal markings doesn't remove the risk.
The picture shows two official signs that cannot both be true for the same stretch of road at the same time, so the only explanation is that the signage itself is contradictory.
The combination of signs shown is the standard advance warning used specifically for a railway level crossing, so that is the hazard a driver should expect after making the turn.

At a crossing controlled by both a barrier and a traffic light, either signal alone can be misleading, so the safe rule is to treat a fully raised barrier together with a green light as the only combination that means it's clear to proceed.

A ball rolling into the road is a classic telltale sign that a child may run out after it, so the safe response is to slow down and be ready to stop rather than just sounding the horn and continuing on.

Reducing speed shortens both reaction distance and braking distance, giving the driver more time and room to spot the pedestrian early and react safely, instead of relying on the horn to move them out of the way.

A pedestrian who looks far away now can close the gap or change direction unexpectedly by the time the vehicle arrives, so the duty of care calls for slowing down and being ready to stop rather than assuming there's nothing to do yet.

The general duty to avoid endangering pedestrians applies even where there is no marked crossing, so slowing down and stopping if needed to let the person finish crossing safely is required, rather than signaling them to hurry.
The pedestrian's safety comes first, so a driver must slow right down and avoid any action, including stopping abruptly right beside them, that could startle them into an unsafe movement.

An opening car door is a common roadside hazard, so the safe response is to reduce speed and be ready to stop, rather than swerving sharply or relying on the horn, neither of which prevents a door that's already opening.

Leaving adequate lateral space from parked cars protects against sudden hazards such as an opening door or a pedestrian stepping out from between vehicles, a risk that a horn or headlights cannot remove.

Parked vehicles along an urban road are a recognized telltale sign of hidden pedestrians who may step out from between them, so the road should be treated as carrying that hazard rather than as clear and surprise-free.

Children getting on or off a stopped school bus may cross unpredictably near the vehicle, so the driver must slow down and be ready to stop instead of overtaking at normal speed or relying on the horn.
The law doesn't ban overtaking a bus loading children outright, but it conditions it on taking every precaution against a child running into the road, not on simply honking a warning beforehand.

A pedestrian who is crossing keeps priority until they've safely finished, so the driver must slow down and stop if necessary rather than assuming the pedestrian will yield just because they've been noticed.

Even when a pedestrian and vehicle are still some distance apart, the responsibility to slow down and stop if needed rests with the driver, since preventing the collision is the job of whoever controls the vehicle.
Pedestrians already on the crossing keep the right to finish crossing safely, so the vehicle must come to a full stop rather than continuing or trying to hurry them along with the horn.
Traffic law restricts horn use to warning of an immediate danger that can't be avoided any other way, not as a general-purpose signal to pedestrians or other drivers.
Stopping on a traffic island blocks the separation area meant to keep traffic flowing safely around it, which is the specific offence shown rather than a lane-position or parking-angle issue.
When several road hazards appear together, reducing speed and keeping to the right side of the lane gives the largest safety margin from both oncoming traffic and the hazards ahead.

Before jacking up a vehicle, the essential safety check is that the vehicle is fully immobilized, since a jack only holds the car vertically and cannot stop it from rolling if it isn't otherwise secured.
Fallen fruit on the roadway reduces tire grip in any weather, not only when the road is wet, so the driver must slow down and drive carefully regardless of recent rain.
A motorcycle riding alongside and slightly behind can sit in a vehicle's blind spot, so before turning right the driver must specifically check for a vehicle that mirrors alone might not reveal.
Where the road ahead curves or crests so oncoming traffic can't be seen, keeping to the right and slowing down keeps the driver clear of a vehicle that might appear from the other direction.

On a section with restricted visibility, such as a blind curve or crest, the real hazard is meeting an oncoming vehicle already in or drifting into your lane, which is the core risk the rules for preventing head-on collisions address.

A lit brake warning lamp signals a fault in the braking system, and since braking is essential to vehicle control, the safe response is to stop immediately rather than continue driving in any way until it's checked.
Reducing speed and moving toward the right side of the lane is the standard response to a hazard ahead, giving the largest safety margin without requiring any unusual maneuver.
For private cars, the standard maximum speed on a non-urban road without a physical median divider is 80 km/h, which is the limit that applies to this road section.
Even where a driver technically has priority, the general duty of care requires watching for a vehicle emerging from a side or dirt road, since that driver may not actually yield as required.

The signs mark entry into a built-up area, so the driver must switch to urban driving rules: a lower urban speed, giving way to traffic from the right at unmarked junctions, and watching for pedestrians who are common in town.

Every vehicle approaching a sharp curve is expected to reduce speed before entering it and stay as far to the right as possible, since that combination keeps enough clearance from oncoming traffic through the tightest part of the bend.
The signs shown correspond to a non-urban road with a physical median divider, where the maximum permitted speed for private passenger cars is 90 km/h.

Because road users such as a cyclist can change direction or wobble unexpectedly, the safe response is to reduce speed and stay alert to any change in their behavior rather than assume they'll hold a steady line.
The winding-road warning sign means a series of curves is coming, so the driver should slow down in advance and keep to the right rather than wait until inside the first curve to react.
When no lane change is being forced on your vehicle, the correct response is to keep driving normally while staying alert to vehicles around you, rather than changing lanes unnecessarily.

A 'special speed' sign requires slowing to the marked speed before the curve begins, and keeping to the right further increases the safety margin, since the sign flags the section as needing extra caution rather than being unlawfully placed.

Because centrifugal force in a turn grows with the square of the speed, the vehicle should already be at a safe speed on entry, hold or reduce it through the bend, and only accelerate again once the wheels are straight after the curve.
Where the road ahead offers a restricted view, keeping to the right and slowing down reduces the risk of meeting an oncoming vehicle in your lane before you have time to react.
Because the roadside stand blocks the designated bus bay, the bus is forced to stop within the traffic lane itself, obstructing the normal flow of vehicles behind it.
Traffic law requires driving in the right-hand lane except when overtaking or turning, so a vehicle unnecessarily occupying another lane is the improper conduct shown here.

Heavy rain is a recognized cause of impaired visibility, and lighting rules for such conditions specifically permit using fog lights to improve visibility for the driver and make the vehicle more visible to others.

When parking, the driver is responsible for making sure that passengers getting out of the vehicle do not create a hazard or obstruction, such as opening a door into passing traffic or the vehicles behind.

The picture combines several factors, wet pavement, reduced visibility, and dense traffic, that together demand extra caution and a larger following gap, matching the rule that difficult conditions require increasing the normal safety margin.

Lighting rules require dimming to low beam in time to avoid dazzling an oncoming driver, and combining that with keeping right and slowing down ensures the driver can still stop safely within the shorter range low beam illuminates.
A cyclist can be destabilized by the air turbulence and proximity of a passing vehicle, so slowing down when approaching them reduces that risk instead of treating them the same as motorized traffic.

Where the road layout ahead is changing with lanes joining or splitting, a driver already in a lane must watch for vehicles merging in from either side, not assume merging traffic will only come from one direction.
When the number of lanes is reducing, moving over to the continuing lane early and keeping to the right avoids a last-moment, higher-risk merge.

A stop sign can be posted to control just one specific movement at a junction, such as a left turn, rather than every vehicle approaching, so only the driver making that particular movement is bound to stop there.
The picture combines three separate signs, so the driver faces all three restrictions together: a work zone ahead, a lower mandatory speed, and a temporary ban on overtaking.
Traffic law requires a motorcycle passenger to keep both feet on the footrests provided on either side of the bike, which is a stability and safety requirement rather than an age limit.
The specific sign combination marking that branch of the road matches the official signage used for the start of a freeway, distinguishing it from an ordinary urban or inter-urban road.
The signage on that branch corresponds to a standard inter-urban road rather than a freeway or a restricted road, based on the sign types displayed there.
The sign warns that traffic can join from the right without having priority, so the driver on the main road must still watch for those merging vehicles even though they are supposed to yield.
Of all road categories, only a freeway permits private passenger cars to drive at 110 km/h, since ordinary non-urban roads and divided non-urban roads carry lower maximum limits.
An officially placed traffic sign carries full legal force regardless of its color, so a yellow sign used for a genuine traffic instruction is just as binding as a white or red one.
The arrow displayed on the sign restricts traffic at that junction to continuing straight ahead, so turning in any other direction is not permitted there.
The sign combination restricts that lane and direction specifically to public transport vehicles going straight, so private vehicles are not permitted to use it.

The no-overtaking restriction in this location is explained by the restricted view of the road ahead, since overtaking blind, such as near a crest or curve, risks meeting an oncoming vehicle before you can see it.

A vehicle stopped on the hard shoulder may have people getting out or debris nearby, so slowing down when passing it reduces the risk of a sudden hazard, matching the duty to account for objects and people near the road.
A vehicle in the process of merging needs room and time to complete the manoeuvre safely, so slowing down gives it the space to do so rather than forcing it into a fast-closing gap.

A heavy vehicle in constrained road conditions needs a larger safety margin and can move slowly or unpredictably, so the correct response is to keep back, slow down, and wait patiently rather than closing the gap.

On a descent combined with a curve, using a low gear lets the engine help control speed through braking, while keeping to the right maintains distance from any oncoming vehicle the limited sightline might otherwise hide.
A continuous line prohibiting overtaking is typically placed where the road ahead can't be fully seen, such as near a crest or bend, so drivers aren't tempted to overtake into a blind stretch.
Based on the priority indicated for that junction, the vehicle without the right of way must yield to the other, regardless of which one arrives or turns first.

A green light only grants permission to proceed; it doesn't remove the driver's duty to watch for pedestrians who might suddenly step out from between parked cars, since the signal can't see or control what pedestrians do.

Where an obstruction, such as a stopped vehicle or an accident scene, narrows the usable road to one lane, the driver must slow down, be ready to stop, and give way to oncoming traffic already using that space rather than push through first.

On a narrow section such as a bridge, priority is given to whichever direction is already closer to or already in the constriction, so the vehicle still farther away must wait even if it might otherwise reach the point first.
A large object like a container standing close to the road blocks the driver's view of anyone who might be crossing from behind it, so slowing down compensates for that lost visibility.
A red light shown together with yellow still means stop; it only signals that green is coming next, so drivers must remain stopped but prepare to move off rather than treat it as permission to go.
Keeping to the right side of the lane through a sharp curve maximizes the clearance from oncoming traffic, so vehicles positioned that way are behaving exactly as the rules for cornering require.

A vehicle that drifts toward the centerline while cornering reduces the space available for oncoming traffic on a curve, which is precisely the hazard that keeping to the right in a curve is meant to prevent.

Failing to hug the right side of the lane through a curve leaves less room for a vehicle approaching from the opposite direction, creating the same head-on risk that the keep-right rule for curves exists to avoid.
Positioning as far right as the road safely allows keeps maximum distance from oncoming traffic and reduces risk, so a vehicle that fails to do so is the fault identified in the picture.

The sign warns that this stretch has no shoulder to pull into if something goes wrong, so the appropriate response is to slow down and stay alert, not to drive faster or shift position within the lane.
Approaching a curve calls for staying on the right side of the lane and entering it cautiously at a controlled speed, rather than maintaining the same speed or moving toward the center.

Since the tanker driver can't see whether the road ahead is clear of oncoming traffic, staying to the right of the lane is exactly the precaution needed, and failing to do so is the fault being illustrated.
A vehicle's brakes slow it down by pressing pads against a disc, converting the car's motion into heat through that friction, which is the basic mechanical principle behind how brakes stop a car.

Repeated or prolonged braking, such as on a long descent, builds up heat in the brakes faster than it can dissipate, and overheated brakes lose stopping power, so excessive use makes braking less effective, not more.

Shifting to a lower gear lets engine braking carry much of the load on a long descent, so only light, occasional use of the brake pedal is needed, preventing the brakes from overheating from continuous use.
When brakes overheat, the friction material loses its grip on the disc or drum, so the direct consequence is a significant drop in how effectively the brakes can slow the vehicle.

Overheated brakes are typically noticed through a lessened, less responsive braking feel along with a distinct smell of burned material, both signs that the friction material is losing its effectiveness.

Once brakes have overheated from continuous use, the safe response is to stop and let them cool down before resuming, then rely on a very low gear rather than immediately demanding full braking power again.
ABS prevents the wheels from locking under hard braking, which keeps the tires able to grip and steer, letting the driver brake hard and still change direction to avoid an obstacle at the same time.

Once a wheel is locked and sliding rather than rolling, it can no longer generate the sideways grip needed to steer, so the vehicle loses its ability to be steered even though the driver turns the wheel.
Wheel locking describes the tires ceasing to rotate and instead skidding along the road surface, which happens when braking force is strong and sustained enough to overcome the tires' grip.
The starter motor's job is simply to spin the engine over fast enough for it to begin firing on its own, after which it disengages and the engine runs under its own power.

A driver checks that a hydraulic brake system is working properly by monitoring the brake fluid level, testing that braking is effective, and noticing any unusual vibration or noise, rather than assuming it needs no attention.

The parking brake typically only holds two wheels and applies far less force than the main hydraulic system, so it lacks the power needed for safe emergency or regular braking and is reserved for holding a stationary vehicle.

Lighting rules require a vehicle's front and rear lights to be lit during hours of darkness or poor visibility, and a single working headlight doesn't meet that requirement, so the driver must not continue until it's fixed.

Because the braking system is essential for safely controlling a vehicle, discovering a fault while driving means stopping right away and having it towed for repair rather than trying to continue, even carefully.
Selecting a low gear on a long downhill stretch lets engine braking do most of the work of controlling speed, reducing the load on the service brakes and lowering the risk of them overheating.
